nothing to collide with, yet the tick wedges permanently on a `cp` whose source does not exist. `backup=empty` is the signature: the resolver DID classify this as a collision (the index still tracks the path) and attempted the backup cp, which failed because a bare `rm` had already taken the file off disk. This is the SAME resolver defect as the del_unstaged x {delete,tree_at_path} rows, not the del_staged fail-safe: those measure `backup=no` because the resolver never touches them and git's own ff-only refuses. The fail-safe reason was copied here in error and is corrected 2026-09-01.

restore_kept_local's `cp -p` targets a path that is now a DIRECTORY, so cp's directory-target semantics copy the file INSIDE it: Pro's authoritative content lands at Subject.md/Subject.md while the tracked path is a directory, and cp exits 0 so the puller logs `restored kept-local Pro-authoritative runtime-state` — a FALSE SUCCESS. Measured against the real puller 2026-09-01: rc=0, that exact log line present, content nested. Any consumer reading the tracked path as a file finds a directory. Verdict corrected from OK.

not allowlisted, so no keep-local restore is attempted at all: the local modification is backed up before the ff and origin's directory takes the path, which is origin's intent. Contrast row 81, where the identical shape under keeplocal produces a false-success restore.

restore_kept_local's `cp -p` targets a path that is now a DANGLING SYMLINK, and cp FOLLOWS it: it creates a regular file at the LINK'S TARGET NAME. Measured against the real puller 2026-09-01: rc=0, cp exits 0, the log says `restored kept-local Pro-authoritative runtime-state`, and an UNTRACKED `bystander.md` appears at the repo root holding Pro's content while `git status` goes `?? bystander.md`. Reading the tracked path does return that content, but only by accident of the link resolving to a file nobody declared. False success, and the next tick meets an untracked file it did not put there. NOTE for anyone re-deriving this: `cp -p` onto a dangling symlink exits 1 ONLY when the target has a missing intermediate directory; onto a bare filename with an existing parent -- which is what the fixture builds -- it exits 0 and follows. A probe using the wrong shape reports the opposite mechanism. Verdict corrected from OK, twice: first from an unargued OK, then back from an OK justified by a loud-failure story measured on the WRONG symlink shape.

not allowlisted, so no keep-local restore is attempted: the local modification is backed up and origin's symlink takes the path, which is origin's intent. Contrast row 83, where the same shape under keeplocal makes cp follow the dangling link and strew an untracked file at the repo root.

no wedge, but `cp -p` DEREFERENCES the link into the backup: recovery returns the TARGET file's bytes under this name with no record it was ever a link, and on a keep-local path the restore writes that regular file back, silently converting Pro-authoritative state from a link into a copy. Hand-verified. The seven measured fields cannot express this, which is why the verdict column is written by a human

two mechanisms compound here. The backup IS dereferenced (`cp -p` reads through the resolving local link). Then the restore targets a path that is now a DIRECTORY, so cp's directory-target semantics nest the file inside it: the final tree holds both origin's `Subject.md/panel.json` and a nested `Subject.md/Subject.md` carrying the dereferenced content, with the log claiming `restored kept-local`. The old reason said the state is 'converted from a link into a copy at that path' — there is no readable file at that path at all, there is a directory with a confusingly-named file buried in it. Same nesting mechanism as row 81, compounded with the dereference.
